senses: According to the required or usual ceremonies, formalities, or rituals; specifically (Christianity, obsolete), to ceremonial laws in the Bible.
Involving much ceremony; ostentatious, showy.
Of a person: fond of ceremony or ritual, or of observing strict etiquette or formality; punctilious.
Synonym of ceremonial (“of, relating to, consisting of, or used in a ceremony or rite”); formal, ritual.
ety: Learned borrowing from Middle French cérémonieux (modern French cérémonieux) or directly from its etymon Latin caerimōniōsus + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)). Caerimōniōsus is derived from Latin caerimōnia (“awe, reverence, veneration; sacredness, sanctity; religious ceremony, ritual”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer- (“to build, make; to do”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, overly’ forming adjectives from nouns). By surface analysis, ceremony + -ous.
examples: He descended to the cabin to bid a ceremonious, and, it may be, tacitly rebukeful adieu.
Ancient and oriental cultures are in many ways more conventional, more ceremonious, and more courteous than our own.

senses: Covered in rime (etymology 1) or (generally) frost.
ety: From rime (etymology 1) + -ed (suffix forming possessional adjectives, and past tense and past participle forms of regular verbs).
examples: The rimed window permitted only shades of the traffic outside.

senses: Flowing; able to flow.
ety: From flow + -y.
examples: In her flowy skirt, with her flowy hair, bare feet, and still the single eyebrow, she reads a poem that sounds like it came straight from English class.

senses: Someone being interviewed, i.e. the person answering the questions.
ety: From interview + -ee.
examples: Both ‘no-op’ interviewees hold relatively stable identities as TG and offer interesting perspectives on trans repudiation from a TG standpoint.

senses: A mail delivery vehicle that also serves as a bus for passengers, typically in areas with limited public transport.
ety: From post + bus.
examples: The novelty value of a postbus ride is even 'sold' in some local tourist offices; the Broadford-Elgol route on the Isle of Skye has acquired particular fame for its spectacular views of the Cuillin Hills.

senses: An instrument for mowing grass, grain, etc. by hand, composed of a long, curving blade with a sharp concave edge, fastened to a long handle called a snath.
A scythe-shaped blade attached to ancient war chariots.
The tenth Lenormand card.
ety: From Middle English sythe, sithe, from Old English sīþe, sīgþe, sigdi (“sickle”), from Proto-West Germanic *sigiþi, from Proto-Germanic *sigiþiz, *sigiþō, derived from *seg- (“saw”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). Immediate Germanic cognates include Middle Low German sēgede, Dutch zicht, Icelandic sigð (all “sickle”). More distantly related with Dutch zeis, German Sense (both “scythe”). Also akin to English saw, which see. The silent c crept in during the early 15th century owing to folk-etymological association with Medieval Latin scissor (“tailor, carver”), from Latin scindō (“to
examples: Early next morning the gudewife took a scythe on her shoulder, and went out in the fields with the hay-mowers to mow.

senses: One who favours independence (of a non-independent state).
ety: From independent + -ist.
examples: The independentists denounced dependency as colonial lackeyism
Between 1939 and 1947 the independentists concerned themselves primarily with the welfare of the Polish majority.
Although a classification of terrorism activities can vary, the most active terrorist groups in those years can be divided into extremist and separatist / independentist movements.

senses: The practice of keeping secrets.
The condition of being hidden or concealed.
ety: From Old French concelement (“concealment, secrecy”). By surface analysis, conceal + -ment.
examples: The documents were hidden in deliberate concealment.
He was charged with the concealment of evidence.

senses: To make public or known; to communicate to the public; to tell (information, especially a secret) so that it may become generally known.
To indicate publicly; to proclaim.
ety: Inherited from Middle English divulgen, from Latin dīvulgō + -en (verb-forming suffix), from dī- (“widely”) + vulgō (“to make known, announce; to publish”).
examples: I will never divulge that secret to anyone.
In an interview with The Economist last year, he insisted his attack on the CPP had nothing to do with his views on global warming, which he would not divulge.
Here then is a letter from a young man whose name I must not reveal, but whom I will designate as D. F., and whose address I must not divulge, but will simply indicate as Q. Street, West.

senses: A child or baby.
ety: Borrowed from Scots bairn, from Middle English bern, barn, from Old English bearn, from Proto-West Germanic *barn, from Proto-Germanic *barną. Doublet of barn. Compare West Frisian bern.
examples: She moved about the country like a ghost, gathering herbs in dark loanings, lingering in kirkyairds, and casting a blight on innocent bairns.
They say that a shag is good for an unborn child, they get the circulation of blood, or some shite. The least ah kin dae is take an interest in the bairn’s welfare.
Bobby Shaftoe's getten a bairn For to dandle in his arm; In his arm and on his knee, Bobby Shaftoe loves me.

senses: To apply or make use of (someone or something); to employ, to use.
To impart (something) gratuitously; to present (something) to someone or something, especially as a gift or an honour; to confer, to give, to accord; to render.
ety: The verb is derived from Middle English bestowen, bistouen, bistowen (“to give, bestow; to apply (something to something else); to arrange or have control over (something); to place (someone) in a position; to use (for some purpose); (reflexive) to find (oneself) a place to live or shelter”) [and other forms], from bi- (prefix forming verbs, often with a completive, figurative, or intensive meaning) + stouen, stowen (“to pack (cargo) in a ship, stow; to place (someone) in a certain position; to provide quarters for, lodge; etc.”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to place; to stan
examples: I bestow upon you the name of Peter.
Medals were bestowed on the winning team.
Soft tears again bedewed my cheeks, and I even raised my humid eyes with thankfulness towards the blessed sun which bestowed such joy upon me.

senses: To invest with dignity or honour.
To give distinction to.
To exalt in rank.
To treat as worthy or acceptable; to indulge or condone by acknowledging.
ety: From Old French dignifier, from Late Latin dignificare, from dignus (“worthy”) + ficare (in comp.), facere (“to make”). See deign and fact.
examples: Your worth will dignify our feast.
Or, when more deeply moved, he would exclaim-- "As noble thoughts the inward being grace, So noble whiskers dignify the face."
I will not dignify that comment with a response.

senses: A frumpy person, somebody who is unattractive, drab or dowdy.
Unattractive, dowdy clothes.
A bad-tempered person.
ety: Probably a contraction of late Middle English frumpylle (“wrinkle”), from Middle Dutch verrompelen, originally equivalent to for- + rump + -le.
examples: You look like such a frump today!
Using the ideal of French female beauty as a stick with which to beat Britain's supposedly sexless frumps is a stereotype centuries old.
If you flipped through certain magazines at this time you could be forgiven for thinking that there was no right way to be a woman, only wrong ones — bimbo or frump, slut or prude, shrew or doormat.

senses: A belt of marshy land, which lies between the foothills of the Himalayas and the plains.
A terai hat.
ety: Borrowed from Nepali तराइ (tarāi) and/or Hindustani (Hindi तराई (tarāī) / Urdu ترائی (tarāī, “marsh, foothills”)), from Prakrit *तलघट्टिका- (*talaghaṭṭikā-), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-Aryan *taras (“plain, plateau”), possibly related to Sanskrit तल (tala, “level”); cognate to Nepali तराइ (tarāi). Possibly later associated with Classical Persian تر (tar, “humid”).
examples: Emotions running high, clashes between protesters and police led to the death of at least 40 people in Terai since August – including 11 police officials, one of them dragged out of an ambulance and beaten to death.

senses: An Italian variant of ice cream made from milk and sugar, combined with other flavourings. The ingredients are supercooled while stirring to break up ice crystals as they form.
ety: Borrowed from Italian gelato (“ice cream”), from Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).
examples: Now the area has been remade in their image. Every other storefront seems to be a coffee shop, a gelato shop, or a med spa.

senses: A traditional Russian fur cap with earflaps.
ety: Borrowed from Russian уша́нка (ušánka), from у́ши (úši) (the accusative or nominative plural of у́хо (úxo, “ear”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws (“ear”), from *h₂ew- (“to see; to be aware of, perceive”) with a shift of meaning) + -а́нка (-ánka) (variant of -я́нка (-jánka, suffix forming names of specific objects)).
examples: I have no idea why he's wearing a ushanka in triple digit heat; bro's forehead must be drenched in sweat.

senses: To move things physically towards the centre; to consolidate or concentrate
To move power to a single, central authority
To make something focal, the most important
ety: From central + -ize.
examples: She examines authors Mary Daly and Andrea Dworkin and criticizes the analysis that centralizes all our oppression in sexism.

senses: Often complaining; suggesting a complaint in expression; fretful, whining.
ety: From Old French querelos, from Late Latin querulōsus, from Latin querulus, from queror (“to complain”).
examples: The nights were now cold, gemmed with a multitude of bright stars, uncanny with the querulous wail of coyotes and the occasional deep voices of wolves.

senses: The antler of a hart, once used as a source of ammonia.
An aqueous solution of ammonia; smelling salts.
ety: From hart + -s- + horn.
examples: Sophia, who had tottered along with much difficulty, sunk down in her chair; but by the assistance of hartshorn and water, she was prevented from fainting away...
Lady Teazle seeing Sir Peter in such Danger—ran out of the Room in strong Hysterics—and Charles after her calling out for Hartshorn and Water!

senses: One of the bowls used in the French game of boules.
A single-crystal ingot produced by synthetic means.
A round loaf of bread.
A round piece of dough.
A through-sawn log with the slices restacked in the order and orientation they originally had in the log, usually with waney edges.
ety: From French boule. Doublet of bull (etymologies 2 and 4) and bulla, or of bowl and pulla, depending on the etymology of the French word.
examples: Behind him is lumber 'sawn in the boule.' Wood is more commonly sawn in this manner in Europe and is stacked in the order it comes from the log.
Specialty lumber dealers can cut and sticker a log "in the boule," so that boards hold the same relative position they had before milling
A live-sawn log kept as a unit is known as a boule

senses: To parade, display with ostentation.
ety: Of North Germanic origin. Perhaps related to Norwegian flanta (“to show off, wander about”), Icelandic flana (“to rush about, act rashly or heedlessly”) and then also to French flâner (“to wander around, loiter”). Alternatively, it could be related to Swedish flankt (“loosely, flutteringly”) (compare English flaunt-a-flaunt), from flanka (“waver, hang and wave about, ramble”), a nasalised variant of flakka (“to waver”), related to Middle English flacken (“to move to and fro, flutter, palpitate”). See flack.
examples: She’s always flaunting her designer clothes.
He pierced with his sombre detachment the plate-glass of ironmongers and saddlers, while Strether flaunted an affinity with the dealers in stamped letter-paper and in smart neckties.
Never one to miss an opportunity to flaunt his wealth, Khashoggi let his yacht be used for the 1983 Bond film Never Say Never Again.

senses: A device that applies stripes.
The striped bass, Morone saxatilis, a popular sport fish native to North America.
ety: * (device): From stripe (verb) + -er (agent noun suffix). * (fish): From stripe (noun) + -er (relational suffix). * (military): From stripe (noun) + -er (suffix denoting a person to whom a certain number of something applies).
examples: We rented a line striper for the parking lot.

senses: A soft, creamy Italian cheese that is not pressed or aged; often used in desserts.
ety: Borrowed from Italian mascarpone, from Lombard.
examples: Chic cosmopolitan design meets authentic pizza Napoletana in more than a dozen styles, including the red sauce capriciosa — with artichokes, Taggiasca olives and prosciutto cotto — and white-sauce speck and mascarpone.

senses: Of a throwback or exhibiting primitivism.
ety: From atavism + -istic.
examples: The true perversion took place only in the privacy of her mind — the way she imagined an atavistic macho atop her when engaged in a mandatory contribution to the fetus-banks with some cretinous inept breeder…
Because I am atavistic enough to believe that drawing is the basic language of the illustrator, even as words comprise the basic language of the writer…

senses: A set of teeth, the teeth viewed as a unit.
An artificial replacement of one or more teeth.
A complete replacement of all teeth in a mouth.
ety: From French denture (“set of teeth”), from Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + -urus, -ura, -urum, a suffix implying a set.
examples: After the mouth surgery, she was fitted with a denture.

senses: The seed-like fruit of the caraway plant.
A cake or sweetmeat containing caraway seeds.
ety: From Middle English caraway, carewey, carwey, from Medieval Latin carui, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā), via Aramaic from Ancient Greek καρώ (karṓ), κάρον (káron, “caraway”).
examples: I'll eat her marchpane and her caraways

senses: A splinter, fragment or chip, especially of stone.
A process of weathering, aging, or other wear that involves the crumbling of the substrate.
ety: From Middle English spalle (“a chip”) (first documented in 1440), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from the Middle English verb spald (“to split”) (c.1400), from Middle Low German spalden, cognate with Old High German spaltan (“to split”).
examples: The failure of this bearing involved spall under high load.
The inspection of this bridge abutment found extensive spall.

senses: A dessert made from ice cream frozen in a (generally spherical or hemispherical) mold.
A small, roughly hemispherical, chocolate-covered confection.
ety: From French bombe. Doublet of bomb.
examples: Sous-chef Daniel O'Reagan prepares an array of tempting desserts, including a zabaglione and marzipan bombe, chocolate mousse torte and an amaretto-flavored cheesecake.
The best dessert by far is the chocolate-caramel bombe, a gorgeous chocolate-dusted dome with a heart of passion fruit crème brûlée.
Austria boasts the Mozart ball, a marzipan-filled chocolate ball wrapped in a portrait of the composer. Niemetz of Vienna also manufactures a famous marshmallow bombe called the Schwedenbombe.

senses: A form of trapshooting using clay targets to simulate birds in flight.
A hand consisting of a 9, a 5, a 2, and two other cards lower than 9.
ety: Pseudo-archaic alteration of shoot, perhaps with reference to Old Norse skjóta; compare Scots skite (“to dart, to shoot”). The name for a form of trapshooting is attested from the 1920s, see quotations below. Senses related to ejaculation of semen likely derive from this, but compare also squirt, skite, or scoot. The word skeet is attested in reference to working class persons in US English from the 19th century, or the Newfoundland and Labrador regionalism may derive from other terms such as skite or skeeter; see quotation below.
examples: THE ARTICLE on the sport of Skeet that appeared in the June issue of WILD LIFE described the layout of the Skeet field, installation of the traps, and the rules and regulations for Skeet shooting.

Skeet started informally in 1920 as off-season practice for bird hunting, so it needed few rules. It became more formally organized in 1926 when the National Skeet Shooting Association (NSSA) was formed.

senses: Having frills, frilly.
ety: From frill + -ed.
examples: The sole image of Henry Cavendish captured in his lifetime shows an aristocratic-looking man in a frock coat, frilled shirt-wrists, and white stockings, wearing a knocker-tailed periwig under a black three-cornered hat.

senses: To enjoy luxury, to indulge.
To be luxuriant; to grow exuberantly.
ety: First attested in 1621; borrowed from Latin lūxuriātus, perfect passive participle of lūxuriō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
examples: Luxuriate in the wonderful service of our five-star hotel.
He luxuriated in anger, and he kept accounts.

But where the stage version luxuriated in the amount of time it could take to tell its story — in three one-act plays — its big-screen counterpart benefits from the need to economize in order to keep things moving.

senses: A device used to scan prepared forms used for multiple-choice and true-or-false testing.
A prepared form for use in such a device.
ety: Genericized trademark. By genericization of Scantron (from scan + -tron), a manufacturer and brand name of the devices.
examples: The Grievant, however, insisted on using the scantron himself.

senses: Resembling an organ of the body.
ety: From organ + -oid.

senses: A cross between a domestic cow and an American buffalo or bison.
The meat of such a hybrid.
ety: Blend of beef + buffalo.

senses: Any of several passerine songbirds, of the family Pycnonotidae (currently, 27 genera recognized), native to Africa and Eurasia.
ety: Borrowed from Classical Persian بلبل (bulbul) or from Arabic بُلْبُل (bulbul).

senses: Not befitting; not appropriate or suitable.
ety: From un- + befitting.

senses: Between developmental stages.
ety: From inter- + stadial.

senses: A person who advises people (normally women) on cosmetics and other beauty treatments; a beautician.
ety: From cosmetology + -ist.
examples: I think cosmetologist is pushing it. Even esthetician has its drawback - sounds too much like "Esteelauder."

senses: A tool used to manipulate logs, having a thick wooden handle, a steel point, and a curved hooked arm. Similar to a cant-hook, but shorter and stouter, and with a pointed end.
ety: After Joseph Peavey, a blacksmith from Maine in the United States of America.

senses: A line or cable that can be shot across a gap.
ety: From gun + line.
